title: Integer Optimization I: The Power of Yes/No Decisions
subtitle: Binary variables, fixed costs, and big-M logic — how one line of code lets your model make strategic decisions, and why that makes it exponentially harder to solve

objectives.title: Model decisions, not just quantities
objectives.description: Use binary variables to encode yes/no choices — open a facility, launch a product, sign a contract — inside an otherwise linear model.

objectives.title: Master fixed-charge and logical constraints
objectives.description: Link binary and continuous variables with big-M fixed-charge constraints, and translate either/or and if-then business rules into linear inequalities.

objectives.title: Build intuition for branch & bound
objectives.description: Explain how solvers search the tree of yes/no combinations, why LP relaxations give bounds, and what the MIP gap in the Gurobi log actually means.

objectives.title: Respect the computational cliff
objectives.description: Understand why integer programming is exponentially harder than LP, and why formulation quality — especially tight big-M values — decides whether your model solves in seconds or never.

agenda.title: Opening: The $50 Million Question LP Cannot Answer
agenda.description: Last week we routed flow through a network we took as given. Tonight we decide what the network IS — and that requires a new kind of variable.
bulletPoints: Why 'build 0.37 of a warehouse' is nonsense: fractional answers fail for strategic decisions
Homework #4 debrief: the lanes you wished you could open or close — now you can
The one-line change: vtype=GRB.BINARY, and what it buys (and costs) you

agenda.title: Binary Variables & the Fixed-Charge Trick
agenda.description: The single most useful modeling pattern in prescriptive analytics: pay a fixed cost only if you use the capacity.
bulletPoints: y = 1 if we open it, 0 if not: fixed costs enter the objective as f*y
The linking constraint x <= M*y: no shipping through a warehouse that doesn't exist
Choosing M: why 'just use a million' wrecks performance and how to pick a tight bound

agenda.title: Logic as Algebra: Either/Or and If-Then
agenda.description: Business rules become linear constraints once you have binaries to switch them on and off.
bulletPoints: Either/or constraints: at least one of two conditions must hold, big-M relaxes the other
If-then: 'if we enter Europe, we must open at least two DCs there' becomes a linear inequality in binaries
Selection logic: at most k of n, mutually exclusive options, prerequisite chains

agenda.title: Break
agenda.description: Ten minutes. When you return: why your laptop can solve some 10,000-variable IPs in seconds and choke on some 50-variable ones.

agenda.title: Branch & Bound: How the Solver Thinks
agenda.description: Inside the search tree: relax, bound, branch, prune. This is why IP is exponentially harder than LP — and why it still works in practice.
bulletPoints: 2^n combinations: 50 binary variables means over a quadrillion-quadrillion possible plans — enumeration is hopeless
LP relaxation as an optimistic bound; branching on fractional binaries; pruning dominated subtrees
Reading the Gurobi log live: incumbent, best bound, and the MIP gap converging

agenda.title: Hands-On: Facility Location with Fixed Opening Costs
agenda.description: Teams build the classic capacitated facility location model in gurobipy: which warehouses to open, and which customers each one serves.
bulletPoints: Binary open/close decisions plus continuous shipment variables
Fixed-charge linking constraints tie the two together
Compare the IP solution to its LP relaxation: see the fractional-warehouse absurdity firsthand

agenda.title: Wrap-Up & Homework #5 Launch
agenda.description: Takeaways, the project-selection knapsack assignment, and a preview of scheduling models and the midterm case.
bulletPoints: Recap: binaries for decisions, big-M for linking, branch & bound under the hood
Homework #5: capital budgeting as a knapsack — pick the project portfolio
Next week: set covering, workforce scheduling, CP-SAT, and the midterm case launch

activities.title: Facility Location: Which Warehouses Do We Open?
activities.description: Five candidate warehouses, each with a hefty fixed opening cost and limited capacity. Eight customer zones with known demand. Your team decides which warehouses to open and how to serve every customer at minimum total cost — fixed plus variable.

steps.title: Declare the two variable families
steps.description: Binary y[w] = 1 if warehouse w opens; continuous x[w,c] = units shipped from w to customer c. Strategic and operational decisions living in one model.

steps.title: Write the fixed-charge link
steps.description: Total shipments out of w cannot exceed capacity[w] * y[w]. Closed warehouse, zero flow — and note the M here is the capacity, not an arbitrary huge number.

steps.title: Solve and read the log
steps.description: Watch branch & bound work: incumbent solutions, the best bound, the gap closing to 0%. Which warehouses opened, and does the geography make sense?

steps.title: Relax and compare
steps.description: Change vtype to continuous and re-solve. The LP happily opens 0.42 of a warehouse and beats your IP cost — an answer that is cheaper and impossible. That gap is the price of reality.

codeBlock.code:
import gurobipy as gp
from gurobipy import GRB

wh = ["W1", "W2", "W3", "W4", "W5"]
fixed = {"W1": 120000, "W2": 95000, "W3": 150000, "W4": 80000, "W5": 110000}
cap = {"W1": 900, "W2": 700, "W3": 1100, "W4": 500, "W5": 800}
cust = {"C1": 240, "C2": 180, "C3": 310, "C4": 150,
        "C5": 220, "C6": 270, "C7": 130, "C8": 200}
# ship_cost[w, c] provided in the class data cell

m = gp.Model("facility_location")
y = m.addVars(wh, vtype=GRB.BINARY, name="open")
x = m.addVars(wh, cust.keys(), name="ship")

m.setObjective(
    gp.quicksum(fixed[w] * y[w] for w in wh)
    + gp.quicksum(ship_cost[w, c] * x[w, c] for w in wh for c in cust),
    GRB.MINIMIZE)

# Fixed-charge link: no flow through a closed warehouse
for w in wh:
    m.addConstr(x.sum(w, "*") <= cap[w] * y[w], name=f"link_{w}")
# Meet every customer's demand
for c, d in cust.items():
    m.addConstr(x.sum("*", c) == d, name=f"demand_{c}")

m.optimize()
opened = [w for w in wh if y[w].X > 0.5]
print(f"Open: {opened}  |  Total cost: ${m.ObjVal:,.0f}")

activities.discussionNote: Notice that the linking constraint used capacity as the big-M — the tightest valid value. Loose M values make the LP relaxation weak, the branch & bound tree explodes, and 'the same model' can go from 2 seconds to 2 hours. In IP, formulation quality is not style — it is performance. Where else tonight could a rule of thumb ('just make M huge') quietly sabotage you?

takeaways.text: Binary variables turn optimization from a calculator into a strategist: open/close, launch/kill, in/out. One vtype change moves you from allocating quantities to making decisions.

Fixed-charge constraints (x <= M*y) and big-M logic are the modeling patterns behind either/or and if-then rules — and tight M values are the difference between models that solve and models that stall.
IP is exponentially harder than LP — 2^n combinations — but branch & bound prunes intelligently using LP relaxation bounds. Trust the MIP gap, not your enumeration instincts.

homework.label: Homework #5
homework.text: Project-selection knapsack: your division has $10M of capital and 12 candidate projects, each with an investment cost, an expected NPV, and staffing needs (data file provided). Build a binary IP in gurobipy that maximizes total NPV subject to the budget and at most 60 staff-months, with two logical rules: Project 7 requires Project 3 (if-then), and Projects 5 and 9 are mutually exclusive (either/or). Report the chosen portfolio, then re-solve with an $8M budget and write 3-4 sentences on which projects fell out and what that says about their bang-for-buck. Colab link due before Session 7.
